claims.claim: Robinson says most Wolfe stories mean whatever the text of the story is, word for word.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: mean whatever the text of the story is, word for word

claims.claim: Robinson catalogues Wolfe's set-piece dialogues as catechisms, interrogations, examinations, Socratic dialogues and classroom lessons.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: catechisms, interrogations, examinations, Socratic dialogues, classroom lessons

claims.claim: Robinson lists anthropological reports among the non-fiction forms Wolfe wrote pastiches of.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: pastiches of anthropological reports, fairy tales, aboriginal tales

claims.claim: Robinson reports Wolfe telling him he chose a sentimental style because the story's idea was sentimental.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson paraphrasing Gene Wolfe, in 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: had a sentimental idea, he chose a sentimental style

claims.claim: Robinson notes the middle novella of The Fifth Head of Cerberus is identified as a fiction written by a minor character in the first story.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: identified as a fiction written by a minor character

claims.claim: Mikalatos argues Wolfe's obscure vocabulary gives the reader more clues to the surrounding world than most fantasies do.
claims.source: Matt Mikalatos, Speculative Faith / Lorehaven, comment 16 March 2013
claims.quote: they give more clues to the world around the reader

claims.claim: Crampton identifies the Latro novels' frame as a manuscript Wolfe merely translates, pointing to the reliability of language.
claims.source: Jeremy Crampton, 'Some Greek Themes in Gene Wolfe's Latro novels', Ultan's Library, 10 August 2000 (written c.1988)

claims.claim: Crampton notes the preface to Soldier of the Mist warns the reader of possible errors of translation.
claims.quote: we are warned against possible errors of translation in the preface

claims.claim: Wolfe's own glossary entry for arete, quoted by Crampton, defines the term by a range running from cleanliness and love of order to courage before death.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, glossary to Soldier of Arete, quoted by Jeremy Crampton, Ultan's Library
claims.quote: ranging from cleanliness and love of order to courage

claims.claim: Wolfe, quoted by Crampton, describes as an error the assumption that one knows what words mean and that they cannot mean anything else.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe in Frontier Crossings (1987) p.119, quoted by Jeremy Crampton, Ultan's Library
claims.quote: one knows what the words mean, that they actually mean

claims.claim: Wolfe's own definition of good literature, quoted back to him by Gaiman from a letter, is writing an educated reader can reread with increased pleasure.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, quoted from a letter by Neil Gaiman in Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: can be read by an educated reader, and reread with

claims.claim: Wolfe describes The Fifth Head of Cerberus as built so that the second novella is a story told by a character in the third.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Neil Gaiman, Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: The second novella is a story told by one

claims.claim: Wolfe says the most important thing fiction does is assure the reader that things need not stay as they are.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Neil Gaiman, Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: it assures the reader that things need not be as

claims.claim: Wolfe grounds his industrial settings in his years as a journalist on a trade magazine.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Neil Gaiman, Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: Remember, I was a journalist on an

claims.claim: Wolfe says the temptation of the defined-terms form is to put one's own prejudices in, as Samuel Johnson did.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Neil Gaiman, Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: put your own prejudices in as Samuel Johnson
